title: Diversity of organisms
introduction: The variety of life challenges us to recognize species, compare chromosomes and interpret the scale and meaning of genome differences.
objectives: Develop an identification key and interpret molecular sampling

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are no two organisms identical in every trait?
sections.explanation:
Organisms show variation in structural, physiological and behavioural traits. Differences result from inherited DNA sequence variants together with development and environmental effects. Continuous variation, such as height, and discontinuous categories, such as some blood-group phenotypes, require different descriptions.

Variation within one population can overlap substantially with variation in another. Classification must consider distributions of traits and multiple diagnostic characters rather than picking one conspicuous individual. Natural selection acts on heritable variation; a trait altered only by the environment is not automatically inherited.

Leaves from a single tree vary with exposure to light; sampling only sunlit leaves would misrepresent total variation.

Compare two leaves from the same tree grown under different illumination: the observed difference is not necessarily an inherited difference. A study of variation should distinguish genotype, developmental environment and measurement error before attributing an observed pattern to evolution.
sections.revisionSummary: Allele differences and differences such as light, nutrition or temperature.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can shared observable traits help identify species?
sections.explanation:
The morphological concept of species groups organisms by combinations of inherited physical traits, including body structures and development. Linnaean taxonomists made widespread use of these characteristics before DNA sequencing was possible. It remains valuable when only visual evidence is available.

A reliable diagnosis uses multiple distinguishing characters and records expected within-species variation. Convergence may produce similar shapes in unrelated species, while different sexes or life stages of one species can look strikingly different.

Male and female birds with different plumage can still be one species; body shape and other characters must also be compared.

An identification based on shape alone may fail when juveniles and adults, males and females, or unrelated look-alikes have different or convergent forms. A defensible morphological diagnosis checks multiple stable traits from representative specimens and records where the criteria are ambiguous.
sections.revisionSummary: Convergent traits, sexual dimorphism, developmental stages or cryptic species.

sections.guidingQuestion: How do the two words of a scientific species name function?
sections.explanation:
A binomial consists of a capitalized genus and a lowercase specific epithet, both normally italicized: Homo sapiens. Several species may belong to the same genus and generally share many related characteristics. The epithet is not a complete unique species name on its own.

Standardized names reduce ambiguity across languages and common names. Taxonomic evidence can justify changing a genus assignment without changing the underlying organism. When writing by hand, genus and epithet may be underlined separately instead of italicized.

Cedrus libani identifies Lebanon cedar: Cedrus is the genus and libani the specific epithet.

The genus label is capitalized, the specific epithet is lowercase, and both words are italicized in typeset text. A scientific name identifies a taxon under an agreed naming convention; it is not evidence by itself that the taxon's evolutionary boundaries are settled.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is reproductive compatibility used as a species criterion?
sections.explanation:
The biological species concept groups populations whose members actually or potentially interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring, while being reproductively isolated from other such groups. Unlike a purely morphological test, it emphasizes opportunities for gene flow.

Separation by geography does not automatically create distinct species. Conversely, occasional hybridization can occur across accepted species boundaries, so fertility data must be interpreted together with broader population patterns. The concept cannot be applied directly to fossils or strictly asexual organisms.

Two separated populations may still be the same biological species if, upon contact, they could reproduce successfully.

Actual or potential natural interbreeding and fertile offspring are useful evidence, but a rare hybrid does not automatically erase all species distinctions. Ecological separation and reduced gene flow may maintain separate lineages despite occasional hybridization.
sections.revisionSummary: Not directly applicable to asexual species or fossils; occasional hybridization can blur boundaries.

sections.guidingQuestion: When can a population boundary become a species boundary?
sections.explanation:
When populations are separated or experience different selection pressures, allele frequencies may diverge through selection, mutation and genetic drift. Differences in mating signals, ecology and chromosome compatibility can gradually restrict gene flow, leading to speciation.

There need not be a single instant at which every criterion changes. Ring-like or partly hybridizing population complexes illustrate why researchers sometimes disagree. Evidence for geographic structure, genetic divergence and actual reproductive barriers should be evaluated together.

Neighbouring populations may hybridize in a narrow zone while those farther apart show marked differences; naming boundaries can be disputed.

A partly separated lineage may retain some gene flow while its inherited traits diverge. Recording the time and criteria used to assign species status matters: genetic clusters, mating tests and distinctive ecology need not change simultaneously.
sections.revisionSummary: Reproductive and genetic differences may accumulate gradually while some gene flow persists.

sections.guidingQuestion: How do typical human and chimpanzee diploid counts compare?
sections.explanation:
Diploid cells generally contain homologous chromosome pairs. Typical human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); typical chimpanzee somatic cells have 48 (24 pairs). Gametes carry a haploid set; humans normally have 23 chromosomes in gametes.

Chromosome number is not a measure of organism complexity or genome size. Evolutionary fusion, fission and ploidy changes alter chromosome counts. Somatic abnormalities and sex-chromosome differences also mean counts should be stated for the sampled cell type, not treated as an absolute for every cell.

A human sperm has 23 chromosomes, not 46, because meiosis halves the number.

Typical human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) and chimpanzee somatic cells 48 (24 pairs). Counts refer to diploid complements in most somatic cells; gametes are haploid and unusual cells can be aneuploid. Equal counts can occur in different species.

sections.guidingQuestion: How is a karyogram interpreted and the chromosome-2 fusion claim tested?
sections.explanation:
Chromosomes are arranged in homologous pairs using length, characteristic banding patterns and centromere position. Each metaphase chromosome may contain two joined sister chromatids; it is still one replicated chromosome before sister separation.

Human chromosome 2 contains large regions corresponding to two ancestral ape chromosomes. Internal telomere-like repeats and evidence of an inactive second ancestral centromere support a fusion model. Sequence alignments and these predicted signatures test the hypothesis more strongly than the chromosome-count difference alone.

In an illustrative pairing task, two similar-length chromosomes with matching bands and centromeres should be paired before counting; colour alone is not a sufficient rule.

The human chromosome-2 fusion hypothesis predicts sequence-level signs: internal telomere-like repeats in head-to-head orientation, remnants of an ancestral centromere and similarity to two chromosomes in other great apes. Chromosome counts alone would not discriminate fusion from unrelated rearrangements.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why do individuals of a species have highly similar but non-identical genomes?
sections.explanation:
A genome is the total genetic information of an organism, including nuclear and organelle DNA where present. Members of the same species share extensive regions of DNA sequence and broadly corresponding sets of genes.

Sequence variation includes single-nucleotide polymorphisms, insertions, deletions and larger rearrangements. Differences can influence phenotypes, but expression and environment also matter. Genome sequence should not be confused with the subset of genes actively expressed in any one cell.

Two people often carry different SNP alleles at the same locus despite sharing overall chromosome organisation.

A SNP is a difference at a single nucleotide position; many SNPs have no observable effect, while others alter coding or regulatory regions. High sequence similarity within a species is compatible with meaningful genetic variation and should not be confused with identical traits.
sections.revisionSummary: A variable single nucleotide at a genomic position contributes to heritable variation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does genome size vary independently of organismal complexity?
sections.explanation:
Eukaryotic genomes vary in nucleotide sequences, chromosome organisation, gene content and total DNA amount. Much of the difference in size comes from repetitive DNA, transposable elements, introns and duplicated regions, not simply protein-coding genes.

The C-value paradox describes the poor correspondence between genome size and apparent organism complexity. Comparisons must distinguish haploid size estimates from assembled genome length, which may exclude difficult repetitive regions.

A plant can have a larger nuclear genome than a mammal without having proportionally more protein-coding genes or cell types.

Genome size is total DNA, not the number of protein-coding genes or the degree of organismal complexity. Repeated sequences, introns, transposable elements and polyploidy all contribute to genome size, making simple size-equals-complexity rankings unreliable.

sections.guidingQuestion: What benefits and limits follow from reading complete genomes?
sections.explanation:
Whole-genome sequencing enables comparison of related species, investigation of population history and identification of candidate variants associated with disease. Sequencing has become faster and less costly per base through technological innovation.

Genomic information can potentially help individualized clinical decisions, but many variants have uncertain effects and diseases are multifactorial. Clinical applications depend on validated associations, patient consent, privacy, appropriate interpretation and access to qualified care.

A clinically validated tumour variant can guide consideration of a targeted therapy; a raw sequence alone does not select a treatment.

A genome sequence can reveal inherited variants or relatedness, but many variants have uncertain clinical significance and predictions depend on population representation. Faster sequencing and cheaper reads do not eliminate the need for consent, privacy safeguards and expert interpretation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does asexual reproduction challenge the biological species concept?
sections.explanation:
Asexually reproducing organisms, including many microbes, do not mate to create fertile offspring. The biological species concept's direct breeding test therefore cannot be applied to them. Fossils create a comparable practical problem because mating cannot be observed.

Bacteria may exchange DNA through horizontal gene transfer even across recognised taxonomic groups. DNA exchange is not the same as sexual reproduction of whole organisms. Phylogenetic, ecological and genomic criteria can offer alternative species definitions that need not always agree.

Two bacterial lineages might exchange a resistance plasmid but remain distinct in most of their genomes and ecological niches.

Horizontal gene transfer moves DNA between lineages without the reproduction assumed by the biological species concept; binary fission likewise provides no interbreeding test. Sequence-based clustering and ecological criteria may be more appropriate, but none gives a universal boundary.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why may hybrids between species with different chromosome numbers be sterile?
sections.explanation:
Consistent chromosome complements within many species allow homologues to pair during meiosis. Hybrids formed from parents with different chromosome numbers or arrangements can experience pairing and segregation problems, generating unbalanced gametes.

Different numbers do not make mating or hybrid development universally impossible. Hybrid fertility depends on chromosome organisation and meiotic behaviour; some plant polyploids regain pairing and fertility. The degree of reproductive isolation needs evidence.

Mules, offspring of horses and donkeys, are generally sterile because their chromosomes pair poorly during meiosis.

Different chromosome numbers can cause unpaired chromosomes or abnormal segregation at meiosis in some hybrids, reducing fertility. This is a tendency, not a universal rule: chromosome rearrangements and polyploid rescue can allow viable or fertile hybrids.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a field observer identify several plants using paired choices?
sections.explanation:
A dichotomous key gives two mutually exclusive alternatives at each decision, ideally based on readily observable traits. Each route leads to a named taxon or another pair of choices. Observers should test the key against specimens and revise ambiguous couplets.

A suggested Lebanon-relevant comparison uses olive (Olea europaea) with broad opposite leaves, Lebanon cedar (Cedrus libani) with needles clustered on short shoots, and a local two-needle pine species with needles in sheathed bundles. These are proposed field identification criteria; no live observations have been made here. Verify the pine species and seasonally reliable traits in the actual sample.

1a Broad opposite leaves → olive; 1b needle leaves → 2. 2a Needles clustered on short shoots → cedar; 2b needles in sheathed bundles → pine (verify species).

Use a reproducible, observable character in each mutually exclusive couplet; avoid characters unavailable in juvenile or seasonal samples. The olive–cedar–pine demonstration is provisional, not a validated inventory of local specimens. Test the same key on new samples and record mistaken endpoints.

sections.guidingQuestion: What does DNA in a habitat sample reveal about the organisms present?
sections.explanation:
Organisms release environmental DNA (eDNA) into water or soil. Researchers extract and amplify or sequence selected marker regions, then compare them to reference DNA barcodes. Animal COI and plant chloroplast markers such as rbcL and matK are examples used for identification.

Signals may be transported or persist after individuals leave, and PCR contamination or incomplete reference libraries can cause false assignments. Detection suggests biological material from a taxon, not the number of living individuals at the exact sampling point. Repeat sampling and negative controls strengthen inference.

Fish DNA collected downstream gives evidence for fish genetic material in the system, but not a reliable local fish count.

Collect field blanks and replicate samples before comparing amplified DNA against a reference barcode library. A positive DNA signal may persist or travel away from its source, while non-detection may be due to low copy number or primer mismatch. Neither a read count nor a positive detection is automatically a population census.

The fertile offspring indicate interbreeding remains possible, so additional natural gene-flow evidence is needed.

questions.prompt: How do typical human and chimpanzee diploid counts compare?

options.text: Humans 46, chimpanzees 48 in typical diploid somatic cells.
options.feedback: Typically humans 46 and chimpanzees 48.

options.text: Humans 48, chimpanzees 46.
options.feedback: Counts reflect chromosome organisation and ploidy, not evolutionary rank.

options.text: Humans 23, chimpanzees 24 in all their cells.
options.feedback: Counts reflect chromosome organisation and ploidy, not evolutionary rank.

options.text: Human somatic cells have 92 separate chromosomes in metaphase.
options.feedback: Counts reflect chromosome organisation and ploidy, not evolutionary rank.

questions.prompt: Why would a biologist not identify an unknown organism to species using only its diploid chromosome count? Give one relevant human–chimpanzee comparison.
questions.answer: Different species can have the same chromosome number, so the count is not a unique identifier. Typical human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes, whereas chimpanzee diploid cells have 48.
markingPoints: Different species can have the same chromosome number, so the count is not a unique identifier.
Typical human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes, whereas chimpanzee diploid cells have 48.

questions.prompt: In the original illustrated chromosome panel A–F, which pairs share length, centromere position and banding?

options.text: A–D, B–F and C–E
options.feedback: These pairs share all three depicted karyotype features.

options.text: A–B, C–D and E–F
options.feedback: A and B differ in their length and centromere, as do the other suggested combinations.

options.text: A–C, B–E and D–F
options.feedback: This mixes different banding and centromere-position types.

options.text: A–F, B–D and C–E
options.feedback: C–E is supported, but A–F and B–D are not matched by length and centromere position.

questions.prompt: An investigator finds 46 chromosomes in humans and 48 in chimpanzees. Name two additional observations that specifically test a chromosome-fusion hypothesis.
questions.answer: Identify internal head-to-head telomere-repeat sequences at the predicted fusion region. Identify evidence of a vestigial centromere and/or chromosome-sequence correspondence to two ancestral ape chromosomes.
markingPoints: Identify internal head-to-head telomere-repeat sequences at the predicted fusion region.
Identify evidence of a vestigial centromere and/or chromosome-sequence correspondence to two ancestral ape chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Why do individuals of a species have highly similar but non-identical genomes?

options.text: Most inherited sequence is shared, but variants create differences.
options.feedback: A variable single nucleotide at a genomic position contributes to heritable variation.

options.text: A genome includes only active proteins.
options.feedback: Species members share most of their genome while retaining many allelic differences.

options.text: Genomes never include mitochondrial DNA.
options.feedback: Species members share most of their genome while retaining many allelic differences.

options.text: Species members differ only in external appearance.
options.feedback: Species members share most of their genome while retaining many allelic differences.

questions.prompt: Two members of a species differ at one DNA base but show the same measured trait. Explain why this does not contradict genomic variation.
questions.answer: A single-nucleotide polymorphism is genuine sequence variation even without a visible trait change. The variant may be neutral, silent or unrelated to the observed trait.
markingPoints: A single-nucleotide polymorphism is genuine sequence variation even without a visible trait change.
The variant may be neutral, silent or unrelated to the observed trait.

questions.prompt: Why does genome size vary independently of organismal complexity?

options.text: Genome size and complexity are not simply proportional.
options.feedback: Repeat/retrotransposon content, duplications, introns or chromosomal changes.

options.text: The longest genome always encodes the most proteins.
options.feedback: Repetitive DNA and genome history can expand size without added visible complexity.

options.text: Every eukaryote has equal sequence length.
options.feedback: Repetitive DNA and genome history can expand size without added visible complexity.

options.text: Repeats cannot contribute to genome size.
options.feedback: Repetitive DNA and genome history can expand size without added visible complexity.

questions.prompt: A flowering plant has more nuclear DNA than a mammal. Explain why it cannot be concluded that the plant is more complex.
questions.answer: Total DNA can include repeats, non-coding regions and extra chromosome sets. Genome length alone is not a valid universal measure of organism complexity.
markingPoints: Total DNA can include repeats, non-coding regions and extra chromosome sets.
Genome length alone is not a valid universal measure of organism complexity.

questions.prompt: What data should support a genome-size graph?

options.text: Record source accessions, units and assembly/size definitions.
options.feedback: Species, accession/source, units, ploidy and assembly completeness or estimate type.

options.text: Only species colour is needed.
options.feedback: Synthetic values must be prominently identified as a model; research data require traceable records.

options.text: Genome size is identical to number of chromosomes.
options.feedback: Synthetic values must be prominently identified as a model; research data require traceable records.

options.text: Use estimated values with no source attribution.
options.feedback: Synthetic values must be prominently identified as a model; research data require traceable records.

questions.prompt: A student mixes 'assembled Mb' from one species with '2C picograms' from another in a genome-size plot. Identify two problems to resolve first.
questions.answer: Convert or clearly distinguish measurement definitions and units: assembly length versus 2C DNA content. Check genome assembly completeness, ploidy and accession provenance before comparison.
markingPoints: Convert or clearly distinguish measurement definitions and units: assembly length versus 2C DNA content.
Check genome assembly completeness, ploidy and accession provenance before comparison.

questions.prompt: What benefits and limits follow from reading complete genomes?

options.text: Evolutionary research is current use; validated personalized medicine is a developing application.
options.feedback: Evolutionary relationship research and clinically validated personalized treatment.

options.text: All sequence differences are harmful.
options.feedback: Genetic risks are probabilistic and interpretation requires environmental and clinical context.

options.text: Genome data never have privacy implications.
options.feedback: Genetic risks are probabilistic and interpretation requires environmental and clinical context.

options.text: Sequencing automatically diagnoses every disease.
options.feedback: Genetic risks are probabilistic and interpretation requires environmental and clinical context.

questions.prompt: A clinic offers a whole-genome report claiming every future disease can be predicted. Give two reasons to reject this claim.
questions.answer: Many conditions depend on environment and interactions among genes, not sequence alone. Variants of uncertain significance and incomplete population evidence limit predictions.
markingPoints: Many conditions depend on environment and interactions among genes, not sequence alone.
Variants of uncertain significance and incomplete population evidence limit predictions.

questions.prompt: Why does asexual reproduction challenge the biological species concept?

options.text: No sexual crossing test exists for strictly asexual lineages.
options.feedback: Asexual lineages do not mate, and horizontal gene transfer is not sexual reproduction.

options.text: Every bacterium mates to make a fertile hybrid.
options.feedback: Horizontal gene transfer does not demonstrate fertile sexual offspring.

options.text: Fossil species can routinely be crossed.
options.feedback: Horizontal gene transfer does not demonstrate fertile sexual offspring.

options.text: One shared plasmid guarantees a single species.
options.feedback: Horizontal gene transfer does not demonstrate fertile sexual offspring.

questions.prompt: Explain why a fertility test cannot classify an asexually dividing bacterium, and name one alternative type of evidence.
questions.answer: Asexually dividing bacteria do not mate to generate the fertile offspring required by the criterion. Use genomic relatedness, ecological coherence or diagnostic traits instead.
markingPoints: Asexually dividing bacteria do not mate to generate the fertile offspring required by the criterion.
Use genomic relatedness, ecological coherence or diagnostic traits instead.

questions.prompt: Why may hybrids between species with different chromosome numbers be sterile?

options.text: Meiotic pairing incompatibility can prevent production of balanced gametes.
options.feedback: Incomplete homologue pairing or segregation in meiosis produces unbalanced gametes.

options.text: All hybrids from different chromosome counts are fully fertile.
options.feedback: Hybrids can develop even when their gamete formation is impaired.

options.text: Chromosome pairing is unnecessary for meiosis.
options.feedback: Hybrids can develop even when their gamete formation is impaired.

options.text: Sterility always comes from a lack of DNA.
options.feedback: Hybrids can develop even when their gamete formation is impaired.

questions.prompt: Two related plant species have different chromosome complements. Predict one possible meiosis problem in their hybrid and state one qualification.
questions.answer: A hybrid may form unpaired chromosomes or unbalanced gametes during meiosis. Different chromosome counts do not guarantee sterility in every cross, especially where chromosome doubling occurs.
markingPoints: A hybrid may form unpaired chromosomes or unbalanced gametes during meiosis.
Different chromosome counts do not guarantee sterility in every cross, especially where chromosome doubling occurs.

questions.prompt: How can a field observer identify several plants using paired choices?

options.text: Use successive observable, mutually exclusive paired choices.
options.feedback: Two contrasting, observable choices that divide the remaining candidate organisms.

options.text: Each choice must have three overlapping alternatives.
options.feedback: It is an identification route based on diagnostic traits, not necessarily phylogeny.

options.text: Use traits that cannot be inspected on the specimen.
options.feedback: It is an identification route based on diagnostic traits, not necessarily phylogeny.

options.text: A key establishes direct evolutionary ancestry.
options.feedback: It is an identification route based on diagnostic traits, not necessarily phylogeny.

questions.prompt: A couplet reads 'plant is attractive' versus 'plant is unattractive'. Explain why it fails and propose a measurable replacement.
questions.answer: Attractiveness is subjective and does not form a reproducible pair of diagnostic states. Use a visible binary contrast, for example broad leaves versus needle-like leaves.
markingPoints: Attractiveness is subjective and does not form a reproducible pair of diagnostic states.
Use a visible binary contrast, for example broad leaves versus needle-like leaves.

questions.prompt: What does DNA in a habitat sample reveal about the organisms present?

options.text: Reference-matched DNA can detect a taxon, subject to controls and interpretation.
options.feedback: Contamination controls, imperfect detection, DNA transport/degradation and incomplete reference libraries.

options.text: Every taxon has identical barcode sequences.
options.feedback: Read abundance is influenced by shedding, degradation, transport and laboratory bias.

options.text: eDNA cannot move through a flowing river.
options.feedback: Read abundance is influenced by shedding, degradation, transport and laboratory bias.

options.text: One negative sample proves a species is absent forever.
options.feedback: Read abundance is influenced by shedding, degradation, transport and laboratory bias.

questions.prompt: Fish DNA is detected in a downstream stream sample. Give one supported conclusion and one unsupported conclusion.
questions.answer: The sample contains DNA associated with the identified fish taxon, subject to controls and database match. It does not prove that a known number of live fish occupy the exact sampling point.
markingPoints: The sample contains DNA associated with the identified fish taxon, subject to controls and database match.
It does not prove that a known number of live fish occupy the exact sampling point.
